observations.details: Cespitose perennial; may be without rhizomes or have rhizomes. Already represented as tufted with possible short underground stems; Gould does not justify a spreading-only score.
Culms described from 50 to 200 cm; this is a broad published range and not a hard rejection criterion.
Culms green or glaucous, freely branching in their upper portion and bearing numerous flowering branches. Branching already scored; color and abundance are new contextual details.

Sheaths strongly keeled and laterally compressed, as broad as 10 mm in some plants but usually considerably narrower. Hairiness ranges from glabrous to villous-pubescent. Existing sheath form and conditional hair mapping retained.
Ligules firm, 1–3 mm long. Matches already source-scored membranous firm ligule; Gould text alone does not separately restate the ligule membrane/edge form in this excerpt.

Basal blades mainly 1.5–4 mm wide, rarely as broad as 6 mm, and 25 cm or longer; linear-tapering with hairiness from smooth to sparse stiff hairs or villous. Width and variable hairiness already represented; minimum length newly retained.
Short flowering racemes mostly 2.5–5 cm long; their architecture is already a primary key clue, numeric interval now retained as a Gould reference.

Rachis joints and pedicels with long silvery cilia at least on the upper two-thirds of these structures. Earlier evidence mapped hairs to the partner stalk; this adds distribution and color without asserting hairs on the spikelet itself.
Sessile spikelets usually 6–8 mm; first glume glabrous or scabrous. True lemma/awn should not be confused with the stalked spikelet partner.

Pedicelled spikelets staminate or neuter, from equal in length to the sessile ones to much shorter; either awnless or bearing a short straight awn. This describes the pedicelled partner, NOT the fertile sessile spikelet awn.
Gould reports 2n=40; cytological report only, not a field-identification or Hays population certification.

Gould's line explicitly says 'lemma 8–15 mm long.' Its organ interpretation requires source reconciliation with other treatments; do NOT silently recode this as true-lemma length or true lemma-awn length.
Only the beginning of the var. divergens couplet is visible below the treatment; the full key was not supplied, and no local subspecies/variety assignment is supported.

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Measure the plant and its lower leaves (Gould)
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: Gould reports stems about 50–200 cm tall, green or bluish-waxy (glaucous); basal leaves typically 1.5–4 mm wide (rarely 6 mm) and 25 cm or longer. Stems may branch repeatedly above. These broad ranges are supporting clues, not exclusive limits.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: season, site conditions, and multiple plants; other grasses overlap these sizes
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Published Texas flora description, not verified for a local specimen; retain variation.

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect the short raceme and its silvery hairs (Gould)
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: Racemes are mostly 2.5–5 cm long. Their rachis joints and pedicels bear long silvery hairs over at least the upper two-thirds. Sessile spikelets are usually 6–8 mm long, with a first glume that may be smooth or rough. Look at intact flowering material with a hand lens.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: silky-haired rachis joints and pedicels versus hairs actually on the spikelet or distant culm nodes
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Gould's published anatomical measurements; no newly verified macrophotograph.

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Check which paired spikelet has the awn (Gould)
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: The pedicelled partner may be staminate or neuter and as long as or shorter than the sessile spikelet; its awn can be absent or short and straight. This does NOT mean the fertile sessile spikelet lacks a true awn. Sheaths may be strongly keeled and laterally flattened, up to 10 mm broad but usually narrower.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: upper fertile lemma awn on the sessile spikelet; do not score the pedicelled partner's short awn as the fertile one
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Gould treatment corroborates the separate-anatomy caution. No automatic key-state changes.

additional_species_treatments.illustration: Fig. 84, Elymus virginicus inflorescence; credited in Gould to Gould and Box (1965)
additional_species_treatments.material: Owner photograph showing printed page 166 and attached engraving, not an independently measured wild specimen

head_decision.rationale: Elymus spikelets sit directly along one unbranched inflorescence axis and their straight/weakly curved lemma awns make the whole spike appear bristly. This is NOT the foxtail/Setaria type of bristles from sterile branchlets below spikelets; compact bristly appearance alone is not evidence of a foxtail panicle.
head_decision.visual_qualifier: Typically stiffly erect even at maturity; the existing 'upright or nodding' category describes the broader single-spike group, not nodding Virginia wildrye specifically.

observations.source_statement: Tufted culms, strictly erect or decumbent at base, mostly 60–120 cm tall; green to glaucous.
observations.details: Habit and culm posture were already characterized in existing evidence. Gould independently corroborates the overall range; a decumbent basal culm does not mean the inflorescence nods.

observations.source_statement: Sheaths glabrous.
observations.details: Gould gives a glabrous condition; H&L permits occasional hairiness. Retain source-specific variation rather than erase the previous conditional character.

observations.source_statement: Minute, truncate membrane.
observations.details: Consistent with the existing membranous-ligule core state; H&L gives a more specific 0.5–1-mm range and possible fine marginal cilia.

observations.source_statement: Flat, glabrous, scabrous, or minutely pubescent; mostly 5–15 mm broad.
observations.details: Matches existing flat blade and measured 5–15-mm width. Skin roughness and fine hairs are variable, not obligatorily absent.

observations.source_statement: Spike usually stiffly erect, often partially enclosed by the upper leaf sheath.
observations.details: Primary basis for keeping 'spike' and clarifying that wheat/rye-like spikes can appear bristly due to awns. This is a single unbranched main axis, not a foxtail panicle.

observations.source_statement: Strongly nerved, indurate, yellowish glumes bowed outward at a nerveless base, with often somewhat curved apex.
observations.details: Hardened, pale U-like expanded glume bases are diagnostic comparative anatomy; a single node alone does not establish species identity where hybrids may occur.

observations.source_statement: Glume apex tapers to a straight awn shorter to longer than the glume body.
observations.details: GLUME awn, not lemma awn; do not conflate their measurement or infer a fixed awn/body ratio.

observations.source_statement: Lemmas glabrous or sparsely hirsute.
observations.details: Variable smooth-to-sparsely-hairy lemma, not necessarily a conspicuously hairy lemma.

observations.source_statement: Straight or slightly curved lemma awn 5–25 mm long.
observations.details: These are TRUE lemma awns, not foxtail's separate sterile branchlet bristles. Relatively shorter/straighter than typical Canada wildrye, but can still be conspicuous. Existing 5–25-mm score evidence preserved.

observations.source_statement: Chromosome number 2n = 28.
observations.details: Published cytological number; not field-identification evidence or proof for a particular Hays specimen.

observations.source_statement: In Gould's 1975 region scheme, occasional in Texas regions except 9 and 10 and more abundant in the eastern half; shaded banks, fence rows and open woodlands.
observations.details: Historical broad distribution/habitat only; NOT modern BONAP Hays County nativity or a local voucher.

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Is it a true erect bristly spike or a foxtail?
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: Gould describes a stiffly erect spike, often partly tucked into the upper leaf sheath. Follow the actual head axis: Elymus spikelets attach directly to it, with straight or slightly curved lemma awns giving the bristly outline. This is not the separate sterile branchlet bristles of a Setaria foxtail.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Setaria foxtails (separate bristles beneath spikelets) and Canada wildrye (often nodding spikes and longer divergent awns)
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Published Texas flora p. 166 plus Texas A&M and USDA descriptions; no identification of a new local specimen.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Frank W. Gould (1975), The Grasses of Texas, Elymus virginicus treatment, printed p. 166

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Check the U-shaped glume bases and straight awns
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: At mature spikelet nodes, inspect the firm, often yellowish, strongly veined glumes; their bases bow outward and lack veins. Gould reports the true lemma awns as straight or slightly curved, 5–25 mm long, with lemmas hairless or sparsely hairy.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Canada wildrye often has sharper V-shaped glumes and longer, outward-curving lemma awns; hybrids can be intermediate.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Source-specific diagnostic features, not a specimen-vouchered determination.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Frank W. Gould (1975), The Grasses of Texas, Elymus virginicus treatment, printed p. 166

additional_species_treatments.material: Owner photograph of Gould's Cenchrus key fragment above the Cenchrus ciliaris species account, plus visible distribution and flowering period

classification_decision.rationale: A dense cylindrical bristly inflorescence supports a foxtail-like outward appearance. Buffelgrass fascicle bristles are mostly fused only at the base and are distinct from lemma/glume awns. Current research-trial head/awn categorization can remain until original-key promotion evidence is independently reconciled.
classification_decision.ligule_note: The book says short CILIATE MEMBRANE with hairs 1–1.5 mm: this is a membranous structure carrying marginal hairs, not evidence for a hair-only ligule. Preserve the current unknown core ligule slot until source-specific mapping and organism-wide candidate promotion is reviewed.
classification_decision.nativity_note: Gould calls it introduced forage grass; do not treat its reported Texas presence or one Hays occurrence as native county flora.

observations.details: Original treatment names Cenchrus ciliaris L. and synonym Pennisetum ciliare (L.) Link. Do not assume any extra synonym or cultivar based on this page.
Perennial; stems erect or knee-bent and spreading, branched and described as 'knotty' at base. Growth form is NOT established from the available research-trial photographs.
Stems 50–100 cm tall in this historical Texas treatment.
Sheaths laterally compressed and keeled, from hairless to sparsely pilose.

Short, ciliate membranous ligule. Gould describes the hairs as mostly 1–1.5 mm long; this is the hair length, NOT an explicit measured height of the membrane itself. Do not transform this into a hair-only ligule score.
Blades thin, usually flat, rough or slightly hairy; mostly 8–30 cm long and 2.5–8 mm broad.
Dense, cylindrical flowering head, mostly 4–10 cm long, occasionally to 13 cm, and 1–2 cm thick. This supports an observational dense bristly cylinder, not a universally identified local specimen.

Purplish bristles 4–10 mm long, cylindrical in cross section (terete), long-ciliate along inner margins, united (connate) only at their bases or slightly above. Separate bristles from glume and lemma awns.
Each fascicle has 2–4 spikelets and a minute, hairy (pilose) peduncle. Count the spikelets inside one bristle-bearing fascicle rather than counting separate fascicles.
Spikelets reported as 2.5–5.6 mm long.
Lemma of the UPPER floret 2.2–5.4 mm long; never map directly to spikelet length or awn length.
Caryopses turgid, ovoid, about 1.4–1.9 mm long and approximately 1 mm in diameter. This describes mature grains, not the entire spikelet.
Gould lists multiple reported chromosome counts, not a specific cytotype confirmed from Hays County.

Gould describes the grass as introduced for forage, then common on sandy rangelands and semi-disturbed sites through Texas region 6, occasionally regions 2, 3, 7, and 10. Historical regional bins are NOT current county-level native distribution.
Gould describes it as native to India and Africa and widely introduced elsewhere. Do not translate this historical generalization into a present-day global distribution determination.
Gould reports flowering from early spring to late autumn under favorable growing conditions. Do not imply a guaranteed Hays County observation window.

adjacent_genus_key_excerpt.scope: Partial Cenchrus key printed immediately ABOVE Cenchrus ciliaris; NOT the C. ciliaris species diagnosis, and the beginning of the key is cut off.

taxa.diagnostic_condition: Burs with one whorl of united flattened spines, subtended by one to several whorls of bristles.
Burs with more than one whorl of flattened spines at irregular intervals; mostly 8–40 spines, larger spine bases often to 1.5 mm wide, upper floret 3.4–5.8 mm.
Burs with more than one whorl of flattened spines at irregular intervals; mostly 45–75 spines, larger spine bases seldom over 1 mm wide, upper floret 5.8–7.6 mm.

adjacent_genus_key_excerpt.caution: Do not apply these spiny-bur species counts as C. ciliaris diagnostic states, and do not treat partial genus couplets as an exhaustive Cenchrus key.

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Measure the dense bristly head (Gould)
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: The buffelgrass inflorescence is a close-packed cylinder, mostly 4–10 cm long (sometimes to 13 cm), about 1–2 cm thick. Its purplish bristles are about 4–10 mm and can look foxtail-like, but inspect the bristles and spikelets rather than identifying by the silhouette alone.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Setaria foxtails and other Cenchrus grasses; confirm whether a fascicle's bristles are united near their bases and how many spikelets it encloses.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Gould published description; Cenchrus ciliaris remains a research trial, with no verified Hays specimen.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Frank W. Gould, The Grasses of Texas, Cenchrus ciliaris treatment, printed page not visible in photograph

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect the ciliate membrane and flattened sheath (Gould)
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: The ligule is a short MEMBRANE with marginal hairs mostly 1–1.5 mm long; this is not a pure fringe-of-hairs ligule. The leaf sheath is flattened and keeled, sometimes bearing sparse hairs; flat blades are mostly 2.5–8 mm wide.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Separate the true membrane from its hairs at the inner blade–sheath junction using magnification; do not measure nearby collar hairs as ligule height.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Published Texas flora source. No new core ligule state scored in the provisional identification key.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Frank W. Gould, The Grasses of Texas, Cenchrus ciliaris treatment, printed page not visible in photograph

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Separate a fascicle and count spikelets (Gould)
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: The bristles are joined only at their bases or a little above. Gould reports 2–4 spikelets per fascicle and spikelets 2.5–5.6 mm long; the UPPER floret lemma is 2.2–5.4 mm. Avoid equating a bristle, a true awn, a fascicle and a spikelet.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Compare whole fascicles with Setaria's separate sterile branchlet bristles and spiny sandbur involucres.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Gould's organism-specific source measurements; dissection and a source-certified local macrophotograph still needed.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Frank W. Gould, The Grasses of Texas, Cenchrus ciliaris treatment, printed page not visible in photograph

additional_species_treatments.common_name: Ryegrass (per Gould); perennial ryegrass in contemporary field use
additional_species_treatments.illustration_reference: Fig. 51 cited with species name; the actual illustration was not included in supplied photo.
additional_species_treatments.material: User-photographed The Grasses of Texas printed p. 106: Lolium genus description, comparative couplet, and complete visible beginning of Lolium perenne species treatment.

observations.details: Annual grasses or short-lived perennials, normally with succulent culms and flat or folded blades.
Genus description gives membranous ligules, often with thin membranous auricles at blade bases.
Spike of several-flowered spikelets, usually one spikelet per rachis node oriented edgewise against a continuous axis.
Separation described above the glume(s) and between individual florets.
First glume usually absent except at terminal spikelet; second glume generally large, several-veined and awnless. These statements are genus-level architecture, not independent specimen verification.
Lemmas described as 5–9-nerved, rounded on back and either awnless or awned from a generally broad tip.
Gould broadly describes the genus as naturally distributed in temperate Europe and Asia. This does not establish individual species nativity in Hays County.

printed_historical_key.details: Glume shorter than the spikelet; long-lived annual or short-lived perennial under Gould's historical species concept.
Glume extends above the uppermost floret; short-lived annual.

genus_context.cautions: Gould's two-species Texas key is not an exhaustive modern Lolium key. It does not distinguish present-day L. multiflorum, L. × boucheanum or all hybrids. Do not turn a historical genus couplet into a negative Hays species filter.
genus_context.adjacent_unrelated_note: The cropped Festuca paradoxa material above the Lolium heading belongs to a preceding species account and was not assigned to Lolium.

classification_decision.rationale: Gould describes the usual erect, unbranched, two-ranked ryegrass spike. He explicitly allows lemma awns to 8 mm, even though the current provisional evidence says typically awnless. The published variation is saved as a separate claim rather than converting an individual plant to an awned or awnless score. Mature spikelet, same-specimen glumes, presence of hybridization, historical species concepts and planting history remain important.
classification_decision.family_scope_note: Gould genus-level traits must remain distinct from species-only observations. Species remains introduced/unverified Hays County research trial; no evidence promotes to the original 112 scored group or BONAP native inventory.

observations.details: Gould describes annual or short-lived perennial, differing in emphasis from the common perennial ryegrass name. Keep wording as printed rather than silently convert to obligately perennial.
Gould reports no rhizomes or stolons. A decumbent culm or basal bunch does not demonstrate a true runner.
Culms 25–70 cm tall; hairless, fairly thick and succulent when green.
Culms glabrous and fairly thick/succulent when green.
Leaves described as glabrous to scabrous and dark green. Do not infer a required smooth leaf surface from one specimen.
Sheaths often have delicate membranous auricles. Genus description also notes thin membranous auricles; do not require their presence on every leaf.
Upper margins of leaf sheath thin and hyaline (translucent), merging near the blade base into a membranous ligule. This is membrane construction, not a hair-only ligule.
Leaf blades 2–10 mm wide; blades may shrink substantially and lose bulk as they dry.
Blades shrivel when dry; measure and describe fresh or properly rehydrated tissue where practical.
Unbranched flowering spike usually 10–20 cm long.
About 15–30 spikelets, one at each axis node, appressed or somewhat spreading and oriented edgewise relative to rachis. Gould's count is a species description, not a strict threshold.
Mostly 5–12 florets within each spikelet. Earlier Kew research packet lists a wider/different range; keep both source-specific.
First glume generally absent except at the terminal spikelet. Compare node position before interpreting single glume status.
Glumes about 5–10 mm long and 1/3–2/3 as long as spikelet with 3–7 strong veins; don't confuse their length with awn or entire spikelet length.
Lemmas approximately as long as glumes and reported five-nerved, with veins generally obscure except toward margins/apex.

Gould explicitly permits either awnless lemmas with blunt membranous tips or lemmas carrying awns up to 8 mm arising from a minutely notched tip. Do NOT automatically assign both positive and negative main-key states or ignore possible taxonomic/hybrid overlap; review anatomical species concept and local voucher first.
Paleas described as about as long as lemmas, with rough (scabrous) surfaces or short hairs (ciliate) along veins.
Gould reports 2n=14; historical literature report only, not a cytological voucher of a Hays population.

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Trace the edge-on spikelets up the ryegrass spike (Gould p. 106)
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: An unbranched spike about 10–20 cm long usually bears 15–30 edge-on spikelets, each at a node along the rachis. Gould reports about 5–12 florets in a spikelet. Look at actual attached nodes: this is a spike, not a foxtail made of separate sterile bristles.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Virginia wildrye has conspicuous glume/lemma awns; L. multiflorum and L. × boucheanum can look similar to L. perenne.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Gould 1975, printed p. 106; literature-only profile, no locally verified voucher.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Frank W. Gould, The Grasses of Texas (1975), printed p. 106, Lolium perenne

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Check the glume, floret and lemma tip together (Gould p. 106)
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: The first glume is normally missing except on the tipmost spikelet; other glumes are usually 5–10 mm long with 3–7 strong veins. Gould describes L. perenne as generally awnless but also allows a lemma awn up to 8 mm from a minutely notched tip. Do not automatically rule the species in or out by awns alone.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Compare whole-spikelet glume proportions, true lemma awns and leaf auricles with L. multiflorum and hybrids; the old L. temulentum couplet is not a complete modern key.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Source-specific variation with species/hybrid interpretation held; identification must use multiple characters.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Frank W. Gould, The Grasses of Texas (1975), printed p. 106, Lolium perenne

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Look closely at the pale membranous collar and soft stems (Gould)
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: Membranous ligule at the inner leaf collar; delicate transparent sheath margins and often tiny membranous auricles. Gould gives 2–10 mm leaf width, 25–70 cm glabrous green culms and a blade that shrivels conspicuously when dried. Paleas may be rough or minutely hairy on their veins.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: A short translucent ligule and clasping ears are different anatomical structures. These supporting clues overlap with other Lolium.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Published Texas species account; supplemental teaching clues, not new scored states.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Frank W. Gould, The Grasses of Texas (1975), printed p. 106, Lolium perenne

taxonomic_crosswalk.verification_status: Kew POWO AND USDA ARS GRIN AGREE
taxonomic_crosswalk.bibliographic_discrepancy: Gould printed Link, Linnaea 9:133, 1835; POWO and GRIN list Link, Linnaea 9:133, 1834. Preserve the original printed date and record the modern bibliographic difference rather than silently rewriting the image.
taxonomic_crosswalk.interpretation: The dated species-level Gould description does not automatically characterize subspp. murinum or glaucum, nor demonstrate which subspecies is represented in existing general H. murinum images and local observation records.
taxonomic_crosswalk.introduced_status: Current Kew distribution treats subsp. leporinum as introduced in Texas. This is not native to Hays County under the project nativity standard, nor proof any individual local record belongs to this subspecies.

classification_decision.reason: Gould's old Hordeum leporinum applies to modern H. murinum subsp. leporinum. Store the morphology on the existing H. murinum research profile with explicit subspecies scoping, not as exclusive states for the entire species complex. No new Hays County subspecies voucher or photo audit.
classification_decision.photo_caution: Existing gallery images labeled H. murinum do not prove subsp. leporinum and should not be relabeled.
classification_decision.history_caution: Gould's historical Texas regional description is not a modern BONAP county occurrence or native-status determination.

observations.details: Gould describes a tufted annual under the name Hordeum leporinum, referring to modern H. murinum subsp. leporinum.
Culms thick, succulent, mostly 15–60 cm tall, usually geniculate-spreading at their lower portions. The bent base is not a nodding flowerhead.
Leaves reported glabrous or more frequently hispid (bearing rather stiff hairs); this must not be recoded as obligatorily hairy.

Ligules truncate (flat-tipped), about 1 mm long. The visible Gould paragraph does not specify ligule construction explicitly, so do not infer a new membrane-versus-hair classification from this sentence alone.
Blades weak and flat, mostly 3–8 mm wide and 6–15 cm long.
Usually with well-developed, slender, pointed auricles at the leaf base; inspect actual clasping structures before deciding their shape.
Flowerhead 4–8 cm long and around 1 cm broad, excluding awns; often partly enclosed in the expanded uppermost leaf sheath.

Florets of lateral spikelets described as large, usually as large as or larger than the floret of the central spikelet. This is Gould's leporinum concept, not necessarily true for every H. murinum subspecies.
Central spikelet floret sits on an elongated rachilla joint about as long as the pedicels of the lateral spikelets; distinguish the rachilla from an actual spikelet pedicel.
Outer glumes associated with the lateral florets are narrow, bristlelike (setaceous), and long-awned. Save printed anatomical wording without conflating glumes and true florets.

Central-spikelet glumes and inner glumes of lateral spikelets are long-awned, broadened/flattened below, with coarse cilia on the margins of that flattened basal portion. A macro photograph is required to confirm that architecture on a specimen.
Glume awns are rough (scabrous), mostly 1–2.5 cm long. Not the 10–35 mm lemma awn described separately.
Lemma BODY 6–12 mm long, gradually tapering to a separate AWN 10–35 mm long. Preserve which organ is being measured; do not add these numbers together as a spikelet length.
Paleas of lateral florets pubescent (hairy), as distinct from lemma or glume hairs.
Stamens of central florets exserted at anthesis (projecting from the flower at flowering time).
Gould reports chromosome number 2n=28; no Hays specimen cytological proof.

Gould says occasional across Texas except the far eastern and southern regions (his regions 1 and 6), and begins describing it as a roadside weed. The remainder continues beyond this photo; no additional habitats should be invented.
Text immediately ABOVE this treatment refers to Hordeum jubatum (foxtail barley), including its separate flowering period and measurements. No Hordeum jubatum traits were assigned to leporinum.

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Hare barley within the wall-barley complex — check the triads
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: Gould's historical H. leporinum is now H. murinum subsp. leporinum. In its flowering spike, the lateral florets may equal or exceed the central one. Check central and lateral spikelet structures at several intact rachis nodes; don't assume every H. murinum specimen is this subspecies.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Other H. murinum subspecies and H. pusillum; require same-specimen close-ups of the central and lateral spikelets before identifying below species rank.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Gould's p. 160 published subsp. leporinum concept plus Kew/USDA name crosswalk; not a locally confirmed subspecies.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Gould (1975), The Grasses of Texas, p. 160 (as H. leporinum); Kew POWO accepted subsp. leporinum

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Separate flattened, ciliate GLUMES from rough awns
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: For Gould's hare-barley treatment, the central glumes and inner lateral glumes are broadened and flattened below, with coarse hairs on the flattened margin. Glume awns are mostly 10–25 mm and rough; lemma bodies 6–12 mm taper to lemma awns 10–35 mm. These are separate organs, not interchangeable lengths.

Fragmentation described as above glumes and between florets; continuous stout rachis is not proof that every cultivated form sheds naturally.

Paleas well developed, about as large as lemmas.
Caryopses ovate or oblong, usually pubescent at the apex. This describes grain tip, not the whole spikelet.
Gould describes embryo as roughly one-fourth to one-third the length of the endosperm, not the whole spikelet.
Published 2n=42; do not treat as chromosome certification of Hays roadside plants.

infraspecific_treatments.variety: Bouteloua curtipendula var. caespitosa Gould & Kapadia

general_species_treatment.details: Strongly keeled laterally compressed sheaths, occasionally up to 10 mm broad, usually narrower. Surfaces smooth to sparsely hairy or villous, varying by form.
Firm ligules measuring 1–3 mm; membrane character corroborated by existing Hill Country and regional flora observations, but Gould does not restate membrane explicitly on these pages.
Linear-acuminate blades; basal blades mostly 1.5–4 mm broad (rarely 6 mm) and at least 25 cm long. Hairless, sparsely hispid, or villous depending on plant/form.
Numerous short racemes mostly 2.5–5 cm; rachis joints and pedicels conspicuously ciliate with silvery hairs over upper two-thirds (hairs may be denser in certain varieties).

Sessile spikelets mostly 6–8 mm; first glume smooth or scabrous. Pedicelled partner staminate or neuter, equal-length to much shorter, usually awnless or with short straight awn; var. frequens and var. virile differ in pedicelled partner structure.

The printed line is retained verbatim only as a short measurement quote from the provided photo; organ attribution needs separate verification. Earlier source held this as a potential confusing lemma vs awn wording. Do NOT recode as fertile lemma or awn length solely from the photograph.
Reported chromosome number 2n=40, not a diagnostic field trait.

infraspecific_key.distinguishing_characters: Lower sheaths and blades densely villous, with long shaggy hairs. Pedicelled spikelets developed, frequently about as long as sessile ones, with two well-developed glumes.
infraspecific_key.flowering_period: August–December reported in the shown variety treatment

infraspecific_key.distinguishing_characters: Creeping rhizomes present; stems and sheaths strongly flattened and sharply keeled; rachis joints and pedicels more or less densely villous.
infraspecific_key.taxonomy_note: This is Gould's historical key name; Kew treats littorale as a name associated with separate Schizachyrium littorale (dune bluestem). Verify spelling and concept before crosswalking.

infraspecific_key.distinguishing_characters: Non-rhizomatous; moderately compressed sheaths, often less sharply keeled; flowering rachis joints and pedicels villous and almost straight at maturity.

Does not produce creeping rhizomes; sheaths and blades hairless or sparsely stiff-hairy; flowering rachis joints and pedicels ciliate but not densely villous; rachis more zigzag and pedicels spreading at maturity. Narrow pedicelled spikelet 1.5–5 mm consisting of a single empty glume.
infraspecific_key.distribution_as_printed: Central, western and southern Texas; statewide except Gould region 1. Particularly in tallgrass prairie openings, rocky slopes, moderate/lightly grazed pastures and rangeland.
infraspecific_key.external_note: Texas A&M Rangelands uses var. frequens for little bluestem across the Edwards Plateau; Kew POWO and ITIS synonymize the name under Schizachyrium scoparium.

infraspecific_key.distinguishing_characters: Non-rhizomatous; flowering rachis ciliate not villous, zigzag with spreading pedicels at maturity; pedicelled spikelets 4.5–7 mm, at least some containing two glumes and often lemma and stamens.
infraspecific_key.source_completeness: The p.609 image shows the heading for the separate variety treatment but NOT its body; retain only characters from the couplet.

taxonomy_crosswalk.kew_powo: Kew Plants of the World Online treats S. scoparium as accepted and var. frequens and var. neomexicanum as synonyms under the species; Kew treats var. virile as synonym of Schizachyrium divergens and var. littorale as synonym of Schizachyrium littorale.
taxonomy_crosswalk.itis: ITIS synonymizes var. frequens to the species but accepts var. neomexicanum and var. virile at variety rank; do not force a single agreed variety taxonomy.

native_locality.species: Native little bluestem occurs in northern Hays County per UT Austin Plant Resources Center field account; BONAP county-level species map also available.
native_locality.variety_assessment: Neither the provided pages nor a species-level county map establishes which Gould variety is native to a particular Hays County site. Do not infer variety-specific local nativity from statewide or ecoregion occurrence.
native_locality.planting_notes: No commercial cultivar, source provenance or nursery plant variety certified by these pages.

nine_main_question_guidance.head: short_racemes (2.5–5 cm) supported; distinguish short lateral silky racemes from one terminal finger cluster.
nine_main_question_guidance.habit: tuft supported; rhizome alternative exists in Gould species concept but creeping rhizomes belong to his var. littoralis. Other listed regional forms may lack creeping rhizomes. Do not require rhizomes for Hays grass.
nine_main_question_guidance.ligule: firm 1–3 mm, membrane status confirmed by existing Diggs and Hagenbuch & Lemke descriptions.
nine_main_question_guidance.awns: Gould 8–15 mm 'lemma' is unresolved organ wording; preserve existing awn observations sourced elsewhere. Pedicelled partner awnless or short-awened does not imply sessile fertile floret awnless.
nine_main_question_guidance.blade_width: Basal 1.5–4 mm typically, rarely 6; crosses thread (<2), narrow 2–5, occasionally medium 5–10. Do not exclude a measured genuine specimen for species-wide typical value.
nine_main_question_guidance.blade_shape: Linear-acuminate is outline, not proof of V-folding or inrolling; retain unknown where those blade states were not directly described.
nine_main_question_guidance.blade_venation: Blade vein/rib category not reported on these pages; leave unknown.
nine_main_question_guidance.blade_hairs: May be hairless, sparse stiff hairs or villous especially eastern varieties. Do not score fixed universal blade hair state or transfer inflorescence hairs to blades.
nine_main_question_guidance.ligule_length: 1–3 mm mostly short, 3 mm measurement boundary overlaps medium. Retain approximate boundary, do not claim long ligule.

classification_decision.source_order: Gould (1975) > Diggs (1999) > Hagenbuch & Lemke (2015), with lower authorities for corroboration; preserve disagreements

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: First recognize little bluestem, not a particular variety
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: Look for tufted growth, short 2.5–5 cm silky racemes at ends of leafy upper branches, paired spikelets and a 1–3 mm firm membranous ligule.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Broader species ID does not establish Gould var. frequens or another variety.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Gould p.608, plus existing regional flora for membranous ligule; Hays specimen/variety unverified.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Gould (1975), The Grasses of Texas, p.608; Diggs (1999), ligule reference

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: For a possible central-Texas var. frequens, examine rachis and pedicel hairs
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: Gould's var. frequens key reports a non-creeping base, ciliate but NOT densely villous flowering rachis and pedicels, a more zigzag rachis, and 1.5–5 mm narrow pedicelled units that are a single empty glume. Compare with dense villous nearly straight western var. neomexicanum.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Requires mature attached racemes and separation of sessile vs pedicelled spikelets. Species-level learner should not force this variety.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Historic Gould key pp.608–609; taxonomic rank not uniformly recognized and Hays voucher unverified.

additional_species_treatments.source: Frank W. Gould (1975), The Grasses of Texas
additional_species_treatments.citation: Gould, F. W. (1975). The Grasses of Texas, printed p.622, Tripsacum dactyloides under genus Tripsacum L.
additional_species_treatments.preservation: All observations paraphrased from the user-uploaded photographed book page. The copyrighted page photo/text and any figures are NOT rehosted; this is a source citation and evidence record, not individual-image rights approval.

observations.details: Perennial forming large clumps from thick, knotted rhizomes; stems about 1.5–3 m tall or taller; culms and leaves described as glabrous.
observations.source_scope: published species description, not authenticated excavated Hays specimens

observations.details: Rounded, smooth and shiny leaf sheaths; glabrous foliage reported.
Short MEMBRANOUS ligule with a ciliate (fringed) or lacerate (torn/irregular) edge. The hairs are a membrane edge characteristic; this does not establish a hair-only ligule lacking membrane.
Thin, mostly flat leaves, usually 10–25 mm wide and 30–75 cm or longer. Numeric range is MOSTLY, not a hard universal min/max; does not exclude anomalous specimens.
Either a single 12–25-cm spicate raceme (spike-like flowering axis) or 2–3 erect spike-like racemose branches, with male (staminate) spikelets above female (pistillate) spikelets.
Upper male spikelets awnless, 2-flowered, usually 6–10 mm long, occurring in pairs on one side of a continuous rachis.

Lower female spikelets usually solitary, subsessile, awnless, usually 6–8 mm. Gould describes hard bony enclosing glumes that become indurate/fused with the rachis, producing distinctive hard shiny jointed units.

On the same p.622 Gould describes glumes of pistillate spikelets first as flat, several-nerved and membranous, then describes their hard/bony indurate condition fused to the rachis. Timing/organ distinction is not explained in the supplied passage; retain both reported descriptions and HOLD exact developmental texture scoring.
Sterile and fertile female floret lemmas thin, hyaline and often reduced; female pedicels/pedicelled spikelets generally absent, occasionally a rudiment.
Upper staminate portion sheds as a unit; lower pistillate portion separates at the nodes into hard beadlike units. Visual hardness cannot be proven from a photograph alone.

Reports Texas throughout but particularly eastern Texas, in low moist relatively little-disturbed grasslands; general eastern-half US distribution west to Nebraska, Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas, plus the West Indies and northern Mexico. Historic state/general range is not a BONAP Hays-county nativity check.
Gould reports April–November in Texas; published interval is not an authenticated current Hays site flowering calendar.
Reports 2n=36, 54, 72, 90, 108 and aneuploid variants in published material; not a routine field identification criterion.

nine_main_question_guidance.head: `mixed_gender` decisively teaches upper male and lower female organs on the same branch. Both single spike-like axis (`spike`) and 2–3 erect terminal branches (`fingers`) are documented positive alternatives, not simultaneously required on each specimen.
nine_main_question_guidance.habit: Tufted large clumps AND thick knotty rhizomes are source-backed for this species; however a photo of a clump does not prove subterranean rhizome identity.
nine_main_question_guidance.ligule: Gould supports ciliate OR lacerate MEMBRANE. Retain existing broad visible membrane/hairs answers provisionally but label any hairlike edge as cilia on a membrane rather than confidently calling it hair-only; inspect exact organ/photo before modifying the broad key.
nine_main_question_guidance.blade_width: Published mostly 10–25 mm supports broad (>10 mm) main picker. The text is MOSTLY, so do not hard-exclude an authentic specimen measured at a boundary or atypical width.
nine_main_question_guidance.blade_shape: Mostly flat blades supported; no claim about rolled/folded variants on this page.
nine_main_question_guidance.blade_venation: No explicit leaf vein or ridge observation in this treatment; do not invent.
nine_main_question_guidance.blade_hairs: Leaves described as glabrous, but no degree-of-hair option should be forced from an isolated head photo or unverified leaf photo.
nine_main_question_guidance.ligule_length: Only SHORT is written; no millimeters supplied here. Do not assign an exact UI measurement bin from this page alone.
nine_main_question_guidance.awns: Both male and female spikelets explicitly awnless. Existing `none_obvious` positive state remains valid.

classification_decision.scoring: Existing core head, growth, ligule and awn states retained; advanced numeric evidence requires safe non-exclusive interval treatment.
classification_decision.staged_female_glume_hold: Same page uses membranous and later indurate/glume-fused language for female spikelets; exact maturity/texture distinction unresolved in photographed passage.
classification_decision.no_county_claim: Gould's historic Texas range does not establish BONAP Hays County nativity or a county voucher.

adjacent_account_boundary.evidence: Page begins separate genus Zea and Zea mays treatment describing cultivated monoecious maize, male terminal and female lateral reproductive heads; the species account is visibly cut off mid-sentence at bottom of supplied page.
adjacent_account_boundary.strict_scope: Do not transfer maize morphology to Tripsacum or treat Gould's historical Zea genus-count assertion as modern accepted taxonomy.

learner_diagnostic_checks.check: Gould p.622: upper staminate spikelets are awnless and 2-flowered, mainly 6–10 mm, paired to one side of a continuous axis; lower female spikelets are generally single and subsessile, 6–8 mm, and the lower rachis breaks into hard beadlike nodes.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Do not call the male paired spikelets female fruits; do not interpret mature bead hardness from photo color alone.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Exact Gould 1975 p.622 morphology, not a local specimen or certified photograph.

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Check leaf width and the inside collar
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: Gould p.622 records mostly flat 10–25 mm blades and a short ciliate or lacerate MEMBRANOUS ligule. Inspect the membrane base: its hairs, if present, are on an edge.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Do not mistake blade hairs for ligule cilia; the published range does not give exact ligule length in mm.

observations.details: Perennial, culms erect to decumbent and hairless, mostly 15–40 cm tall.
Leaf sheaths described as glabrous (without hairs).

Gould describes 'a ciliate crown' of hairs reaching 2 mm. This is the HAIR fringe length, not necessarily the height of an underlying membrane. H&L (2015 p.42) independently report a truncate membranous ligule 1–2 mm with ciliate margins; retain both source descriptions and verify tissue at the inner collar before making a type or length score correction.

Leaf blades up to 15 cm long, usually about 2–3 mm wide. Gould describes surfaces glabrous to scabrous (smooth/hairless to rough); scabrous roughness alone is NOT evidence of ordinary blade pubescence.

Panicle has 10–16 laterally spreading spikelet-bearing branches (racemes) about 5–15 cm long, distributed among 2–5 whorls (verticils) often spaced at least 5 mm, with a frequently erect terminal branch.
Spikelets close to and pressed against the raceme axis, tawny in color, spaced apart with roughly 4–7 spikelets per centimeter of rachis.
Lance-shaped thin membranous glumes, glabrous apart from a scabrous midvein. First (lower) glume about 2–3 mm; second (upper) glume 2.8–3.5 mm.
Lemma of lower floret elliptic to lanceolate, 2–3.5 mm; keel glabrous, margins appressed-pubescent; apex acute to obtuse. Awn of this lower floret 4.8–9 mm.
observations.important: A hairless keel does not make the entire lemma hairless; separate surface parts.

observations.details: One upper sterile floret, oblong and somewhat inflated, truncate at apex, glabrous, length 1.1–2.3 mm; awn 3.2–7 mm.
observations.contrast: Do not confuse the upper sterile lemma/awn with the fertile lower floret/awn or C. cucullata hood.

observations.details: Gould reports chromosome count 2n=40. A literature count, not visible field morphology.

Gould historical Texas Regions 5, 7, 8, 9 and 10. Heavy sandy or gravelly soils in disturbed areas, roadsides, lawns and parks; general central US ranging approximately Nebraska/Iowa through Colorado, Texas, New Mexico and Arizona. Neither the old region list nor a statewide report proves a BONAP Hays County native occurrence.
Gould reports May–September flowering.

Gould notes extensive hybridization with Chloris cucullata where both grow together, including large populations with intermediate plants. This is not an identification or local hybrid confirmation for any particular specimen.

nine_main_question_guidance.flowerhead: `whorls` strongly supported: 10–16 racemes in 2–5 separated whorls, 5–15 cm long. `one_sided` and `many_one_sided` are supported by previously saved Diggs/FNA; do NOT infer one-sided spikelet insertion from Gould's 'appressed' alone. Keep multiple broad alternatives valid.
nine_main_question_guidance.growth_form: Erect to decumbent perennial supported. Existing tuft/mat states come from other verified vegetative and growth evidence; Gould p.321 does not establish true stolons from 'decumbent' alone.
nine_main_question_guidance.leaf_collar: Gould's ciliate crown (cilia to 2 mm) is a published appearance. The existing short ciliate MEMBRANE type is documented in H&L p.42. The new Part A should recognize visible hairs without converting a ciliate rim into a pure hair-only anatomical claim.
nine_main_question_guidance.awns: Long conspicuous true awns: lower fertile lemma 4.8–9 mm, upper sterile floret 3.2–7 mm. Trace attachment separately; keep 'long' main state.
nine_main_question_guidance.leaf_width: Most blades 2–3 mm per Gould, agreeing within H&L published 1–3 mm. Because the 2-mm threshold overlaps `thread` and `narrow`, do not force single bin.
nine_main_question_guidance.leaf_shape: No folded/flat cross-section stated on this page. Existing H&L folded character stays as separate regional evidence, not overridden.
nine_main_question_guidance.leaf_veins: No blade vein character from this page; glume scabrous midnerve is NOT a leaf midrib trait.
nine_main_question_guidance.leaf_hairs: Gould says glabrous to scabrous; roughness does not equal true hair. Keep no forced hairy blade choice.
nine_main_question_guidance.ligule_length: Gould reports HAIRS up to 2 mm, not membrane height. Existing H&L membrane 1–2 mm remains separate measured evidence; do not change numeric filter from Gould.

core_character_verification.assessment: Core shape and awn states agree; both historical hair-fringe appearance and separate H&L membrane anatomy must be explicitly distinguished. A field observation with one head should not diagnose C. verticillata against hybrid C. cucullata without mature spikelets.
potential_future_advanced_review: Compare lower fertile lemma smooth-keel vs pubescent margins and existing conditional smooth whole-lemma option
Check ciliate membrane vs Gould ciliate crown in true inner ligule photographs; do not hard-exclude from new edge selection
No blade vein or new blade hair score from this page

classification_decision.priority: Gould Texas description retained separately from Diggs reproductive and Hagenbuch & Lemke vegetative evidence. Do not silently resolve differences.

learner_diagnostic_checks.check: Gould p.321 describes 10–16 spreading racemes, 5–15 cm each, in 2–5 whorls separated by at least about 5 mm, usually ending in an erect upper branch.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Hooded windmillgrass (*Chloris cucullata*) often has shorter, more crowded branches, but hybrids can have intermediate forms.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Gould printed p.321; a head silhouette or presumed hybrid alone never certifies species identity.

learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Compare hooded windmillgrass's more rounded hood-like sterile lemma and generally shorter awns; verify an intact mature floret before naming a specimen.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Gould p.321; no new dissection photo or ruler verified.

learner_diagnostic_checks.check: The page reports cilia to 2 mm but no distinct membrane-height measurement. H&L p.42 describes a 1–2 mm membrane with a ciliate rim. Use the Leaf collar Part A and B separately and don't label the 2 mm cilia as membrane height.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Ligule character can be shared by *C. cucullata* and windmillgrass intermediates; whorled head and mature floral organs still matter.

observations.details: Tufted perennial with slender weak culms densely grouped into small clumps; usual height 15–40 cm, reported extremes 10–50 cm.

Gould describes the ligule as a minute fringe of short hairs. No numerical length or explicit statement that membranous tissue is absent. Preserve H&L p.38 and opposing FNA/UT tiny ciliate-membrane descriptions; do not silently settle anatomical conflict.
observations.source_disagreement: FNA and UT Austin describe a minute ciliate membrane; direct Gould supports hair-fringe appearance but does not explicitly deny a membrane.

observations.details: Narrow blades flat or somewhat involute (margins rolled inward), generally 4–12 cm long, occasionally to 17 cm, 1–2 mm wide, typically sparsely pilose (long soft hairs).

Axis 3–6 cm above the lowest branch; branches together with their spikelets form wedge-shaped units, usually bearing 3–5 spreading, closely set spikelets, sometimes only 2. Fig.180 illustrates a short sequence of separate bristly, wedge-like lateral branches on the upper stalk, not a long series of dangling oat-like branches. Text does not state exact branch count in this treatment; do not confuse spikelets per branch with branches per head.
observations.figure_scope: One illustrated inflorescence only; not a universal numerical or orientation claim.

observations.details: The printed branch-length phrase reads mostly 0.8–1.6 mm including the awns. On the same pages the branch rachis is 4–7 mm and reduced-floret awns 5–10 mm. These cannot be reconciled as a literal complete-branch length. Possible printing-unit error; do not silently replace mm with cm or score using this interval. Kew prior independently documented 8–16 mm racemes.

Branch rachis 4–7 mm, hairy at base and sparsely hispid above it; tip deeply forked or three-parted. The branch separates as a whole approximately 0.5 mm above its base, leaving a persistent small stub on the main axis.
One perfect (bisexual) floret plus one greatly reduced upper floret. Do not count these as two fertile florets or assign a universal count overriding documented reduced-floret variation elsewhere.

Very unequal glumes; second (upper) glume large and sparsely appressed-pubescent with a stout central nerve extending into a short stout awn between two slender pointed apical lobes. Distinct from the fertile lemma awns.

Body usually 2.5–4 mm, glabrous or sparsely hairy. Two stout short spreading lateral awns plus slightly longer central/terminal awn from between teeth of a notched apex; exact individual awn lengths not stated here.
observations.awn_description: two short spreading lateral awns, slightly longer terminal awn

observations.details: Vestigial upper floret commonly reduced to an awn column and three awns measuring 5–10 mm. This is distinct from the fertile lemma's short awns.
Narrowly obovate, flattened caryopsis with embryo approximately two-thirds as long as endosperm.
2n=40 as reported by Gould.

Gould reports Texas broadly except region 1 and extreme western Texas; grasslands, grassy woodland openings, road rights-of-way, moist slopes. General historical range Oklahoma and Texas south into Coahuila and Tamaulipas. Not county-level voucher evidence or a substitute for BONAP.
April–November in favorable growing conditions, as reported by Gould.

nine_main_question_guidance.flowerhead:
`short_side_racemes` confirmed: compact set of wedge-shaped bristly lateral branches; Fig.180 shows the distinctive overall architecture. `side_oats` specifically identifies numerous pendant/reflexed oat-like branches rather than all lateral units. Field pilot selected side_oats expecting Texas grama and observed its exclusion; propose clearer label contrast (few short bristly wedge/bell-shaped branches vs many dangling oat-like branches on long stalk). Existing Diggs/GrassBase supports 6–8(–10) nonpectinate and unilateral branches; review `one_sided` / `many_one_sided` with exact source and option definition separately, no unilateral claim solely from this illustration.
Resolution: clarified labels and verified Kew exact-species unilateral and 7–10 branch report, enabling `one_sided` and `many_one_sided` as alternate observations; seven-plus conditional; preserve Gould's unit discrepancy separately.
nine_main_question_guidance.growth_form: Tuft strongly confirmed. Gould does not explicitly settle rhizomes/stolons on these pages; preserve H&L/FNA vs UT conflict, no silent score change.
nine_main_question_guidance.leaf_collar: Gould supports minute fringe of short hairs as highest-priority appearance evidence; maintain minute membrane alternative with source conflict until exact tissue verified. Do not artificially make cilia on membrane a pure hair-only identity.
nine_main_question_guidance.awns: Fertile lemma has two short lateral awns and a slightly longer terminal awn; retain `three_short` compatible with other measured evidence; reduced floret 3 awns 5–10 mm are different organs. `none_obvious` is a broad field appearance not a claim of awnlessness.
nine_main_question_guidance.leaf_width: 1–2 mm confirmed; preserve approximate 2-mm boundary and existing interval protection.
nine_main_question_guidance.leaf_shape: Flat and somewhat involute confirmed; not a V-fold assertion.
nine_main_question_guidance.leaf_veins: No blade venation reported; glume midnerve is not blade midrib.
nine_main_question_guidance.leaf_hairs: Usually sparsely pilose, so blade hairs can be present, not required on every specimen.
nine_main_question_guidance.ligule_length: Minute qualitative fringe only. Existing H&L under 0.5 mm and FNA 0.2–0.3 mm are separate quantified evidence.

source_boundary_holds.note: Fig.179 and distribution/flowering text above numbered section 6 refer to B. aristidoides rather than B. rigidiseta.

classification_decision.primary_source_note: Gould affirms tuft, tiny hair fringe, flat/involute blades, sparse hairs, 1–2 mm width, wedge-shaped branches and organ-specific awns. Existing rhizome and membrane alternatives retained with their explicit conflicts; no absence inferred from omission.
classification_decision.branch_length_hold: Printed 0.8–1.6 mm inconsistent with longer branch rachis and upper-floret awns; numerical branch length withheld pending independent verification.
classification_decision.local_nativity: Existing PASS kept; no new county or local specimen identity claims from Gould.

Lemma about same length as glumes; surface may be glabrous, scabrous, or rarely finely puberulent. Lemma usually awnless but an occasional lemma bears an awn up to 3(–4) mm. Do not conflate lemma hairs with short hairs on upper leaf blade.
Palea a little shorter than lemma; anthers about 1.5 mm; chromosome count 2n=20.

observations.source_statement: Densely cespitose perennial; erect culms 30–100 cm, minutely puberulent to scaberulous below nodes.
Sheaths rounded, glabrous or scaberulous.
Ligules firmer below, membranous toward upper portion, 4–12 mm long; ligules of lowermost blades shorter.
Blades elongated gray-green, 25–60 cm long, 1–2 mm wide, involute (rolled inward), scabrous (rough). Scabrous is NOT automatic proof of visible blade hairs.
Dense narrow-contracted panicle 10–30 cm long, about 1 cm across, often interrupted toward base; branches mostly 1–2 cm, closely appressed or ascending.
Spikelets 4–5 mm; glumes obtuse, slightly rough, 2–3 mm.
Lemmas 4–5 mm, rough above, with a few short closely appressed hairs on the CALLUS; usually awnless or awn to 4 mm, rarely longer. Callus hairs are NOT leaf-blade hairs.
Anthers about 2 mm; chromosome number not reported.

Gould records Texas Region 10, Guadalupe Mountains, higher-elevation rocky hills/canyons; Western Texas/New Mexico to northern Mexico; flowering September–November. This is NOT a Hays County locality or BONAP county confirmation.

Gould compares M. metcalfei as a distinct species in this treatment: purplish panicles; branches to 5 cm; glumes 1.5–2 mm; usually 5–10 mm lemma awns. These figures belong to M. metcalfei, not M. dubia.

Gould cites a 1970 treatment synonymizing M. metcalfei with M. dubia, but current Kew POWO (2026) lists M. metcalfei as a synonym of M. rigida; preserve historical disagreement rather than synonymizing automatically.

observations.source_statement: Perennial with a firm NONRHIZOMATOUS, strongly cespitose base and strictly erect 50–100 cm culms.
Stem nodes pubescent; leaf sheaths, especially lower ones, finely pubescent. Do not treat these as blade hairs.
Blades elongated, usually 2–3 mm wide, flat or (more often) inward-rolled; glabrous or finely pubescent.
Narrow contracted panicle usually with 4–10 widely separated, strictly erect branches, each about 1.5–3 cm long.
Panicle axis and branches ciliate/villous; some axis/branch hairs reach about 2–4 mm. These are not leaf hairs and not proof of long lemma awns.

Spikelets ovate, 3.6–4.2 mm; glume and lemma of LOWER floret appressed-hirsute and awnless; lemma of UPPER floret firm and finely rugose, with minute awn tip. Do not combine lower and upper floret surfaces.
Chromosome number 2n=54.

Gould lists Texas Regions 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 (prairies and grassy openings); general range Oklahoma, Texas and northern Mexico; April (occasionally March) through November flowering. A natural-history range description is NOT a BONAP county record.
Gould describes it as palatable forage persisting under moderate grazing and remaining on heavily grazed pasture chiefly where shrubs provide protection.

The photographed Gould p. 433 species treatment does NOT supply a true ligule length or margin description. Do not invent it from the book page. Independently, Hagenbuch & Lemke (2015), exact Eriochloa sericea account, printed p.50, reports a CILIATE ligule to 1 mm with minute membranous base.

cautions: The genus Panicum starts lower on the photographed p.433; its generic anatomy and other Panicum species do not belong to Eriochloa sericea.
No ligule length is described by Gould p.433 itself; 1 mm MAX is verified separately from Hagenbuch & Lemke (2015) p.50.
Do not confuse 2–4 mm hairs on the panicle branches with awns, true ligule cilia, or the (sometimes absent) hairs on leaf blades.
Lower floret glume/lemma hairs and upper fertile floret roughened minute awn belong to distinct floral structures.
A tiny ciliate membrane base may look like a hair fringe to a beginner; do not infer a long papery membrane from the `membrane` conditional visual core state.
